questions.prompt: Which program does the actual computing when you run code?
questions.explain: R is the engine; RStudio is the dashboard you drive it from.

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes the three tools correctly?
choices: R is the language, RStudio is the workspace, and R Markdown is the document format.
RStudio is the language, R is the workspace, and R Markdown is the document format.
R Markdown is the language, R is the workspace, and RStudio is the document format.
R, RStudio, and R Markdown are three names for the same program.
questions.explain: Keep this sentence in mind: R is the language, RStudio is the workspace, R Markdown is the document format.

questions.prompt: You can install RStudio first and R later, in either order.
questions.explain: Install R first, then RStudio. RStudio can't run any code until R is installed.

questions.prompt: In which RStudio pane would you look to see the variables currently in memory?
questions.explain: The Environment pane lists every variable you've created. It's the first place to look when debugging.

questions.prompt: In which pane does R run a command the moment you press Enter, but nothing you type is saved?
questions.explain: Experiment in the Console, and keep what works in the Editor.

questions.prompt: Where should you write code you want to keep and run again later?
questions.explain: Anything in the Editor can be saved in a file and run again.

questions.prompt: What file extension does an R Markdown document have?
questions.explain: R scripts end in `.R`; R Markdown documents end in `.Rmd` (Quarto files end in `.qmd`).

questions.prompt: Which part of an R Markdown file holds the title, author, date, and output format?
questions.explain: The YAML header sits at the top between two lines of three dashes and holds metadata about the document.

questions.prompt: What happens when you **knit** an R Markdown file?
choices: R reruns every code chunk from the top in a fresh session and builds a finished report.
R runs only the chunks you've changed since the last knit.
RStudio saves the file without running any code.
R copies the results from your Console into the document.
questions.explain: Because knitting starts fresh, a file that knits is a file anyone can reproduce from scratch.

questions.prompt: A variable you created only by typing in the Console will still exist when you knit.
questions.explain: Knitting runs in a fresh R session, so it only knows what the file itself creates.

questions.prompt: In Markdown text, what does wrapping a word in double asterisks, like `**word**`, do?
questions.explain: Single asterisks make italic, double asterisks make bold, and a line starting with `#` is a heading.

questions.prompt: When you knit, where does R look for the data files your code reads?
choices: Relative to the folder where the `.Rmd` file is saved
questions.explain: Keep all course files in one `geog215` folder so the `.Rmd` file and its data stay together.

questions.prompt: Quarto `.qmd` files use the same YAML header, Markdown text, and code chunks as R Markdown.
questions.explain: Quarto is the newer successor to R Markdown, made by the same developers.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explain: `months * years` is 1200, and dividing by 10 gives 120.

questions.prompt: What happens when you run this code?
questions.explain: Variable names are case-sensitive: `Months` and `months` are different variables.

questions.prompt: Which character starts a comment in R?
questions.explain: R ignores everything after `#` on a line.

questions.prompt: In `round(3.14159, digits = 2)`, what is `digits = 2`?
questions.explain: Arguments go inside the parentheses. Naming one, as in `digits = 2`, says which input you're setting.

questions.prompt: Complete the code so it rounds to 2 decimal places.
questions.explain: The `digits` argument tells `round()` how many decimal places to keep. Type `?round` to see its help page.

questions.prompt: Complete the code to store 12 in a variable named `months`.
questions.explain: `<-` is the assignment operator. Read it as "gets": months gets 12.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explain: `max()` returns the largest value in the vector.

questions.prompt: What does `c()` do in `c(71, 75, 68)`?
choices: Combines the values into a vector
questions.explain: `c()` combines values into a vector, a sequence of values R stores together.

questions.prompt: What does the pipe `|>` do?
choices: Passes the result on its left as the first argument to the function on its right
Stores the value on its right in the name on its left
Runs the line in the Console instead of the Editor
questions.explain: Read the pipe as "and then". It lets you write nested steps from left to right.

questions.prompt: Rewrite `round(sqrt(max(temps)), digits = 1)` with the pipe. Put the tiles in order.
questions.explain: Take `temps`, and then find the maximum, and then take the square root, and then round.

questions.prompt: Put the tiles in order to store three temperatures in a variable named `temps`.
questions.explain: The value on the right of `<-` is stored in the name on the left.

questions.prompt: Create a variable named `hours` that holds the number of hours in a week (7 days of 24 hours). Let R do the multiplication.
questions.explain: `hours <- 7 * 24` stores 168. Storing values in well-named variables makes code easy to read.

questions.prompt: `temps` holds five daily highs. Store their average in a variable named `avg_temp`.
questions.explain: `mean()` takes a vector and returns its average, 74.2.

questions.prompt: Use the pipe `|>` to take the square root of the sum of `c(4, 9, 16)`, rounded to 2 decimal places. Store the result in `answer`.
questions.explain: The sum is 29, its square root is 5.385..., and rounding gives 5.39.
